nodeData.note: How to count the goods a business holds, compare the count with the books, sort out the differences, and put the right value on the stock. Written for people already doing it at work, with a duka and a pharmacy example.

children.note: A stock take is a physical count of every item the business holds for sale or use. You count it, check its condition, and compare the result with what the records say.
Going round the shelves and store and counting every item by hand or scanner, on one date. It proves what is really there.

manas.q: What is a stock take?

children.note: Goods held to sell, goods being made, and materials used to make them. In a duka it is soap, sugar and airtime; in a pharmacy, medicines.

manas.q: What is inventory?

children.note: Closing stock goes on the balance sheet and lowers cost of sales. A wrong count means wrong profit, so the count must be right.
Theft, breakage, expiry and record errors only show up when you count. The sooner you know, the sooner you can stop the leak.
If you use stock software (a perpetual system), the count tests whether the system's numbers can be trusted.

manas.q: What is a perpetual inventory system?

children.note: Auditors, banks and SACCO lenders want proof that the stock in the accounts exists and is worth what you say.

children.topic: Periodic system: count gives cost of sales
children.note: With no running stock records, cost of sales = opening stock + purchases − closing stock. Example: 80,000 + 420,000 − 95,000 = KES 405,000.

manas.q: How is cost of sales found under a periodic system?

children.note: Most count problems come from poor planning. Plan two to four weeks ahead for a full count.
Usually the year-end date, or as close to it as possible. Pick a quiet time, such as after closing or on a Sunday.
One or two pages telling everyone how to count, where to write, what to do with damaged goods and who to ask. Give them out before the day.

manas.q: Why issue written count instructions?

children.note: Draw a simple plan of shelves, store rooms and fridges and give each area a code. Every area gets a team and a sheet.
One person counts, one writes and checks. Where possible, at least one person should not be the usual storekeeper.

manas.q: Why count in teams of two?

children.note: Sheets or tags with printed serial numbers. Record which numbers each team gets and make sure every one comes back, even if spoiled.

manas.q: Why are count sheets pre-numbered?

children.note: Mark goods held for customers, supplier consignment stock and returns waiting collection. Count them separately so they are not added to your stock.
Cut-off means the count and the books must agree on the same moment in time. Goods move every day, so you draw a line.
Every receipt and sale up to the count time is in both the count and the books; nothing after it is in either.

manas.q: What is cut-off in a stock take?

children.note: Stop receiving and issuing goods during the count. If you must keep trading, put new deliveries aside and count them separately.
Write down the last goods received note (GRN), last delivery note and last sales invoice before the count. Later, check the books stop at the same numbers.

manas.q: Why record the last GRN and invoice numbers?

children.note: If the sale is already invoiced, the goods belong to the customer. Do not include them in your count.
Goods on the road may or may not be yours. It depends on the delivery terms; check who owns them at the count date.
The count itself: careful, steady and documented.
Counters are not shown the system quantity. They write what they see, so they are not tempted to match the book figure.

manas.q: What is a blind count?

children.note: Once an area is done, stick a mark or tag on it. This stops items being missed or counted twice.
Write the unit you counted, such as single bottles, packs of 10 or cartons of 24. Mixing units is a top cause of big errors.
Write down damaged, expired, near-expiry and slow-moving items on the sheet. They may need a lower value later.
A supervisor recounts a sample. Pick some from the sheet and find them on the shelf, and some on the shelf and find them on the sheet.

manas.q: What are the two directions of test counts?

children.note: If a test count or a big variance shows a gap, recount that area with a different team before anyone leaves.
Check every numbered sheet is back, signed by both counters and the supervisor. Make copies before anyone types them in.
Stock that cannot be sold at full price must be valued lower. The count is the best time to spot it.
Items with few or no sales for months. Compare the count with sales history to find them.
Past its use-by date and cannot legally be sold, common in pharmacies and food shops. Usually written down to nil and disposed of properly.
Still sellable but only at a discount soon. It may need a write-down to what you can now sell it for.
Broken packs, old models or out-of-fashion goods. Value at what they can be sold for, less costs to sell.
After the count, compare item by item with the system. The difference is the variance, and each big one must be explained.
Counted quantity minus system quantity. Negative means stock is missing; positive means more than the books show.

manas.q: What is a stock variance?

children.note: Multiply the unit difference by unit cost. Look into the biggest values first, not just the biggest unit counts.
Sales or receipts not recorded, items keyed to the wrong product code, unit mix-ups, cut-off errors, damage and theft.
Check delivery notes, sales records and recounts first. Only post a loss when you cannot find a record error.
Stock that is gone without a record, through theft, damage or error. It is a cost to the business.

manas.q: What is shrinkage?

children.note: A manager signs off the final variance list before the system is adjusted. This stops staff hiding their own losses.
Invented businesses with KES figures. Check each journal: debits equal credits.

children.note: Three product lines in a hardware shop. Compare each line separately.

IAS 2 Inventories sets how to value stock. IFRS for SMEs, used by many small Kenyan firms, has the same main idea.
Stock goes in the books at whichever is lower: what it cost, or what you can get for it (net realisable value).

manas.q: How does IAS 2 measure inventory?

children.note: Expected selling price, less any costs to finish the item, less the costs of selling it.

manas.q: What is net realisable value?

children.note: Purchase price, import duties you cannot recover, and transport to bring goods in. Plus conversion costs if you make the goods.

manas.q: What is included in the cost of inventory?

children.note: Selling costs, abnormal waste, general office costs and storage that is not part of making the goods. These are expenses.

manas.q: Which costs are excluded from inventory cost?

children.note: Use first in, first out (FIFO) or weighted average cost. LIFO is not allowed under IAS 2.

manas.q: Which cost formulas does IAS 2 allow?

children.note: Compare cost and NRV for each item or close group of items, not for all stock in one total.

manas.q: Should cost and NRV be compared in total or item by item?

children.topic: Write-down goes to cost of sales
children.note: A fall to NRV is an expense in the period it happens. If NRV later rises, the write-down can be reversed, up to original cost.
You can count everything once a year, or count a small part every week so all of it is covered over the year.
Everything counted on one day, usually at year end. Simple, but trading often has to stop.

manas.q: What is a full (wall-to-wall) count?

children.note: A few items counted on a regular rota, so the whole store is covered over time. Needs a good perpetual system.

manas.q: What is a cycle count?

children.topic: ABC: count the costly items more
children.note: Group items by value. A items (high value or fast-moving) are counted often, C items (cheap, slow) less often.

manas.q: What is ABC analysis in cycle counting?

children.note: No big shutdown, errors found sooner, and staff get used to counting well.
Only if the system is reliable and the counts are well run and recorded. Otherwise a year-end full count is still needed.
When stock is material, the external auditor usually comes to watch the count. ISA 501 covers this.
When inventory is material, the auditor should attend the count if practical, to see that stock exists and is in good condition.

manas.q: Which ISA covers attending the inventory count?

children.note: Whether staff follow the count instructions, keep cut-off, and separate damaged and other people's goods.
The auditor counts a sample both ways (sheet to floor and floor to sheet) and keeps a record to check later against the final list.
The auditor notes the last GRN and dispatch numbers to test cut-off in the books afterwards.
Watch for these at work and in exams.
Turns the count into a tick exercise. Use blind counts.

manas.q: Why should counters not see system quantities?

children.note: Writing 10 when it was 10 cartons of 24. Always write the unit of measure.
Invoiced goods awaiting collection or supplier consignment stock are not yours. Leave them out.
Gains on some lines hide losses on others. Always compare item by item.
A variance may be a record error. Investigate first, or you hide a real problem.
